title: Meet India's feisty Gen Z protester who is taking on Modi
content: When India's Gen Z-led protesters return to Delhi this weekend for demonstrations seeking the resignation of the country's top election official, one of the prominent faces at the forefront will be that of a 29-year-old PhD student. Neha Bora is a theatre artist and activist who has been with the All India Students' Association (Aisa), a Left-wing organisation known for campus politics, for the past decade and been its president for the past two years. But Neha's - who uses "they" and "them" as personal pronouns - visibility is no longer limited to campuses. Viral videos over the past few days show them being dragged through the street by a group of female police officials, climbing on top of police barricades, raising their fist and shouting slogans, and being detained. Photos of them smiling while being carried away by policewomen have also gone viral. In a recent BBC Bangla interview , Neha played down the attention they've been receiving. "I know it happened in front of the camera so it seems like it's something different," they said. "But I have seen all student activists with the Left doing the same things that I have been doing. It's just that there is a camera on me, so people think something different is happening." The attention on Neha comes at a time when several high-profile protests are being held on India's streets in what is being seen as one of the biggest challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 12 years in power. There's the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a Gen Z-led online satirical movement - that held weeks-long protests in Delhi in the summer over education reforms. It ended in July only after education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation. Separately, some of India's opposition parties, especially the Congress, have also taken to the streets over electoral reforms. For the past few days, videos of Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra being shoved and jostled and detained have gone viral and made headlines in India. Saturday's protest in Delhi has been called by the CJP, which is seeking the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating electoral rolls to favour Modi's BJP. Both the Election Commission and the BJP have rejected the accusation. Although not a member of the CJP, Neha has said their group would also participate. Born in the northern state of Uttarakhand, Neha lived in different cities as a child as their army officer father moved for his postings. After graduating from Delhi University, they did a master's degree from Ambedkar University in the capital and are now a PhD student at the prestigious Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU). Neha first came into the spotlight in the summer during the CJP's protest over education reforms. Neha and Aisa were at the protest from the start, but not many knew them at that point. That changed after 28 June, when educationist and scientist Sonam Wangchuk began a hunger strike in CJP's support and Neha and a few others from Aisa also joined him. "It was an obvious choice for us. We've been protesting against paper leaks and education reforms for a long time," Neha later said in an interview. While most of the attention was focused on Wangchuk, whose reputation and presence galvanised the movement, Neha's outspokenness and combative speeches began to get them noticed. After Wangchuk and others were moved to hospital , Neha continued fasting despite having lost 8kg. Even after being moved to hospital, they said in a video: "The fight continues. Once I've recovered, we'll meet you again on the streets to continue our fight for our right." After the protests ended in July, Neha has established themselves as a Gen Z leader who's courted by the CJP and media, besides appearing alongside Rahul Gandhi at press conferences. But Neha's involvement with Aisa and leftist politics and statements criticising PM Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and other BJP leaders have also led to "lots of disagreements with my family as my parents are staunch supporters of BJP". And last month, at least three police complaints were lodged in Uttar Pradesh state by BJP against Neha for making "objectionable remarks" against the chief minister - they came two days after Aisa's police complaint that Neha had received death threats . Neha, who has been travelling to many Indian cities to participate in protests in support of students, also made headlines when a man allegedly threw ink at them during a protest march in Jharkhand state. A photo Neha shared on Instagram showed their face streaked with ink stains. Police said they had detained the man. The noisy protests and repeated detentions have earned Neha a reputation for being a street fighter. "The streets have always dictated the course of politics in this country and they will continue to do so, more so in the coming few years," they told BBC Bangla. "If we look at the social changes of the recent past, those social changes did not come from people sitting in parliament; they came from the streets," they said. Now as the authorities gear up for 10 October's protest at Jantar Mantar against CEC Kumar, Neha and Aisa have said they would be back in the streets with the CJP to "protect democracy". title: Why is it so hard to put out Indonesian fires shrouding the region in toxic smog?
content: Wildfires have been burning throughout parts of Indonesia for weeks, sending smoke across the country and into neighbouring Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines. The BBC’s Gavin Butler explains why the fires are so difficult to battle and produce so much toxic haze. Thailand’s Queen Suthida made her first solo flight in a fighter jet, according to the Thai Royal Household. The municipality building in Baglung was left teetering on an unstable ledge due to floods before it fell into a river. Days of near continuous downpours have caused widespread flooding in the Thai capital. The BBC is in Inner Mongolia where dozen of Chinese data centres are being constructed, as the country aims to lead the world in artificial intelligence. Lian Yunzhi broke the women's world record twice in three days at World Cube Association competitions. Verified footage appears to show a cargo ship colliding with a fishing boat near Singapore, with investigators still working to establish exactly when and how the crash happened. The BBC goes inside a fortified storage facility to view luxury goods seized by police that are now up for auction. Rescuers are searching for survivors after the vessel travelling from the mainland to a popular tourist destination caught fire. There are still hundreds of workers trapped in a network of tunnels that run along the Trishuli river. BBC South Asia correspondent Azadeh Moshiri is in Nepal where authorities are trying to begin rebuilding amid the debris. Galaxy Robot Park is a 16,500-square-meter venue in South Korea, with attractions including humanoid robots dancing to K-pop hits. The BBC's Tokyo correspondent Kurumi Mori tries Japan's latest food trend, instant noodles made using cold water. Wildfires in Indonesia have destroyed part of the natural habitat of hundreds of orangutans, risking the survival of the species. The BBC reports from Sano Barkhu, a village overlooking the town of Syfrubesi, which was destroyed by the Nepal flooding. Rescue dogs searched for flood victims in Tibet while authorities worked through the night at a Nepal power plant where hundreds are missing. A 17-year-old boy has gone viral for wearing a superhero costume while volunteer firefighting in Indonesia, as the country faces a super El Niño. Thousands in Nepal are still waiting to be rescued, but unpredictable weather is making such operations increasingly difficult. Footage of the flash floods have become almost impossible to find on China’s heavily censored internet. A 97-year-old woman, Guna Maya Bohara, survived the flash floods and was rescued using an excavator. title: Three men found guilty of murdering two Australian surfer brothers and US friend
content: Three men have been found guilty of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024. The men's full names could not be given for legal reasons, and they were only identified as Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús. They are yet to be sentenced - but are likely to spend the rest of their lives in a prison. Debra Robinson, the brother's mother, told the courtroom in the northern Baja California state the murders of her sons had taken "the future we had imagined with them". During the trial the court heard the tourists were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck in a secluded beach area. Their bodies were later found with gunshot wounds to their heads, dumped down a well. The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the coastal area is usually safe from the violence in other parts of Mexico. Debra Robinson and her husband Martin Robinson have been at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial and they delivered emotional testimony during closing arguments before Friday's verdict. "It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," said Martin. Family members of Rhoad joined the trial by video link. Speaking to media outside court a week ago, Debra Robinson said the couple were "deeply grateful" to Australians for the outpouring of support they had received and that they "feel the love and their arms around us". During the month-long trial, the prosecution had sought 150 years in prison for each of the three defendants. In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, Jesús Gerardo alias "El Kekas", was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery. At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings. The beach town has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers and the chilling murders revealed much about how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico. The only explanation the authorities appeared able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time. Their killings took place barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week when their families were able to identify them. At the time, the surfer community in Ensenada turned out in force to commemorate the men by paddling out at one of the area's best known surfing spots and throwing flowers into the sea. Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California. Amid the demands for action, Baja California Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila tried to ease public fears about the widespread violence in her state. "Baja California is and will continue to be a state with safe tourism for the thousands of people who visit us from the rest of the country and the world", she said. "I send my condolences and solidarity to the families at this difficult time." The US president told a rally he had "never heard of" the winner, former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay. title: US country music star Ella Langley cancels show due to 'security threat'
content: US country music star Ella Langley has said she had to cancel her sold-out concert in Tulsa, Oklahoma on Friday night, due to a "serious security threat". The singer made what she called the "incredibly difficult" decision around two hours before the show at the 19,000 seater arena was due to start. In a post on Instagram, the 27-year-old said the threat involved "the safety of my fans, the venue staff and my team". Cpt Richard Meulenberg from Tulsa Police Department said a person had called saying "great harm" would be done at the event with "shots fired and bombs." He stated his team had checked the venue at BOK Center several times before the show and "could not find any threat". "The event was ready to go," he added, saying officers with sniffer dogs did a sweep of the arena again after the phone call was made. "We could not find a credible threat," he said, stressing that the person who had made the call "disrupted this entire event" for thousands of Langley fans. The star - who did not give any further details - also apologised to her fans, saying additional information regarding ticket refunds "will be shared as soon as possible". BOK Center issued its own statement, saying that "the safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed. "We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologise to fans who planned to attend." In September, Langley's country smash Choosin' Texas overtook Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas Is You to become the longest-running number one single in US chart history. Its success helped the singer from Alabama to sweep the Academy of Country Music Awards in May. The planned firing-squad execution on 3 December has led to questions about legality and purpose. title: Life-threatening Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida
content: Hurricane Isaias has made landfall in the US state of Florida and is expected to bring life-threatening flooding and winds that have forced thousands to evacuate. The storm weakened slightly to a category 2 hurricane, with 110 mph (175 kph) winds, before ramming into Florida's western panhandle on Friday evening. Florida, Alabama, and Georgia have each issued states of emergency as meteorologists warned of life-threatening storm surge that could cause up to 9 feet (2.7m) of flooding in some areas. Isaias is one of three storm systems affecting North America this weekend, with the two others hitting Mexico and Southern California in the El-Niño fuelled warm waters of the Pacific Ocean. Both Florida and Alabama instituted mandatory evacuations due to the storm. In Florida, those evacuations includes coastal communities in direct aim of the powerful storm. Florida Senator Rick Scott encouraged residents in designated areas to evacuate as soon as possible, as he warned in a social media post: "DO NOT WAIT! Get out NOW!" Governor of Alabama Kay Ivey issued a mandatory evacuation for all non-residents, tourists and visitors in key counties likely to be heavily affected by the storm. Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific. It marks the first time in more than 30 years that a hurricane did not form till October. The storm is likely to bring "life-threatening storm surge" to the US Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center warned. After hitting Florida, the centre of Isaias is forecast to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on Saturday and Sunday, the National Weather Service said late on Friday. As of Friday evening, hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 35 miles (55 km) from Isaias' centre, and tropical storm-force winds extended as far as 205 miles (335 km). The Florida Panhandle and the rest of the US Gulf Coast are facing fierce winds and heavy rain as the hurricane barrels down. There is also the potential for accompanying tornadoes, Melissa Watson, a Florida-based meteorologist at the National Weather Service told the BBC. For those who have not evacuated, "the main thing will be having multiple ways to receive warnings" about tornadoes and storm surges, Watson said. "If you are near the coast, being able to move to higher ground," is also essential in the event of storm surges. "We want people to be safe, so don't go out there trying to look for damage ... to post on social media," she added. "We want people to remain inside and safe while the hurricane is moving through." Even before the storm made landfall, hundreds of thousands were without power in the country's southeast - and Alabama, Florida and Georgia have issued states of emergency as they brace for heavy rains and flooding. More than 350,000 were in the dark in Florida and another 170,000 in Alabama saw outages, according to PowerOutage.us. The hurricane's winds are expected to be felt further inland in Georgia, albeit at a lesser intensity, where already about 8,000 customers were without power. People on the coast of the Florida panhandle have been told to seek immediate shelter under an "Extreme Wind Warning". Some Florida officials have ordered residents to "Get out NOW!", urging people to follow evacuation orders. John Guoth, a resident of Navarre, Florida, told the BBC that he and his wife will remain in their home despite the rest of his street having already left. "It's a hurricane, we get them all the time... we kind of knew that when we moved here," he said. "Pretty much everything that can fly and will fly is battened down, and everything that cannot fly is really, really secured," he said, Guoth said he put his ducks and chickens in the bathroom and weighed down his boats and trailers so "nothing flips over". A few households have remained in the area, describing them as "long-term locals" who are "going to protect our homes". Pensacola resident Brandin Ruth told the BBC that they have been turning the gas off to the buildings, icing down product and trying to get team members home. People in the Florida city have "seen bad storms before" but are "bunkering up", he said, adding: "You don't want to underestimate a storm like this". One indicator of a storm's severity to communities in the southern US is whether the stalwart restaurant chain The Waffle House would close its doors to customers. On Friday, it did. A Waffle House spokesperson confirmed to the BBC that the chain had already closed a number of locations in the hurricane's path and "will continue monitoring conditions". US President Donald Trump said he will no longer attend a major American football college game in Tuscaloosa, Alabama because of the hurricane, shifting plans to attend a rally in Tennessee instead. Two other storms are also forecast to batter North America this weekend. Hurricane Simon is bearing down on the Pacific coast of Mexico as a category one hurricane. It is set to pick up speed and become category four by Saturday, eventually making landfall near Puerto Vallarta on Sunday, according to Reuters. Further north, Tropical Storm Rachel, a downgraded hurricane, is heading toward landfall around the US-Mexico border, along the Pacific. While, Rachel is expected to reach the coast late on Saturday, the impact of the storm is already being felt due to high tides in southern California. Video footage and photos show several streets under water in Newport Beach, California, through a combination of the tropical storm swells at sea and high tide. Posting on its account on X, the City of Newport Beach advised people to "avoid the Balboa Peninsula due to street flooding caused by recent storm conditions and elevated tides". It also urged people not to drive through flooded streets. Bulldozers have been shoring up the beach to try and prevent further flooding. With additional reporting by Simon King. title: Thousands of security personnel deployed as Delhi braces for ‘cockroach’ protest
content: Parts of the Indian capital, Delhi, have been turned into a fortress, with tens of thousands of security forces deployed, as the influential Gen Z-led "cockroach" movement has called for a major protest on Saturday. The protesters are seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists. The Election Commission has denied this and Kumar is yet to comment on calls for his resignation. The protest comes just months after the movement brought thousands of young people onto Delhi's streets in July, in demonstrations that saw violent clashes with police and forced India's education minister to resign. Police say they have denied permission for the gathering and all roads leading to Jantar Mantar, the main protest venue, have been closed with huge metal barricades. The restrictions have caused major disruption across central Delhi, with traffic diverted from several key roads. A journey that would normally take 15 minutes took more than an hour this morning. At Jantar Mantar, metal barricades and ropes have been erected around the protest site, preventing people from entering. Some protesters who arrived early were stopped and questioned by police and paramilitary personnel deployed in the area. At a nearby roundabout, loudspeakers repeatedly broadcast appeals for people to cooperate with the police. In a late night post on X, Delhi Police on Friday defended the measures, saying they were necessary to maintain public safety and prevent overcrowding at Jantar Mantar, which can accommodate only 1,000 people at a time. Several trains to Delhi have also been cancelled and police have ordered dozens of metro stations shut to prevent protesters from gathering. But Abhijeet Dipke, founder ⁠of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) - the online satirical movement that is spearheading the protests - has said the CJP will march to Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning "come what may". "If you want to jail us or even shoot us we are prepared," he added, addressing ​Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a post on X. The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations demanding education reforms over the summer. The resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in July was seen as a major victory for the group. CJP protesters returned to the streets last week with a rally in Mumbai to demand Kumar's resignation. On Thursday, they held another large rally in the southern city of Bengaluru (formerly Bangalore). Student groups and opposition parties have also protested in the capital over the past few days. Saturday's protests are being billed as the biggest in recent times as they are also being supported by several opposition parties, farmer organisations and student groups. CJP leaders allege the authorities have been preventing many of their supporters from reaching Delhi. In the capital, more than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed and authorities have appealed to citizens to stay away from protests. Police official Nupur Prasad told a press conference that one of the reasons for denying permission to protest at Jantar Mantar was the "short notice" given by the CJP. "Under current guidelines, an application to organise an event at Jantar Mantar must be submitted at least 10 days prior to the scheduled date," she said. Also, she added that in the past, the CJP had not followed "lawful directions" given to them. "In light of the non-compliance with prescribed procedures, the failure to adhere to past legal directions, and the current state of public safety, law and order, and traffic regulation, permission for the proposed protest at Jantar Mantar is hereby denied." The CJP have questioned police denying them permission for the protest - they say that legally they only have to inform the police and do not need their approval to gather. At the centre of the row is a controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year. The Election Commission says it is to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list. But opposition parties and activists have alleged that many of those are eligible voters and that the process is being manipulated by CEC Kumar to favour Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations. The past few days have also seen a major escalation in the opposition's standoff with the Election Commission. For three days in a row starting Tuesday, Delhi witnessed dramatic scenes with police breaking up protests by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other MPs over the issue. Videos showing police forcing Gandhi on to a bus and preventing him from climbing out of the bus window subsequently went viral on social media. title: JD Vance casts doubt on firing squad execution and says he will not watch it
content: US Vice-President JD Vance has cast doubt on the Pentagon's plans to livestream a firing squad execution of the Fort Hood attacker. Vance expressed uncertainty to reporters about whether the December execution would go ahead as planned, saying: "I don't know that that's actually going to happen". He added, that "if it's through live stream, I'm not going to be watching it". Hours later, President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved the live stream plans but the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it. Nidal Hasan killed 13 unarmed soldiers at a base in Texas in 2009, injuring another 32. The firing squad execution would be the first military execution in more than 60 years. The Pentagon announced earlier this week it would execute Nisan, a former US Army major, on 3 December by firing squad in the attack on the Fort Hood base. Then on Thursday US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be livestreamed for the public. "People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth explained. Trump, as he left the White House on Friday, was asked about the possibility that visuals of Hasan's execution could be used as propaganda for terrorists. "He killed 13, 14 people, badly wounded 20-some-odd people, and he's totally nuts," Trump said. "So I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him." The Pentagon declined to comment further when asked for more information about a decision on the livestream. Speaking to reporters on Friday, Vance condemned Hasan's attack on the base as "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11". Asked about how his Catholic faith impacted his stance on the plan to stream a public execution, Vance questioned whether it would happen. But he noted that Hasan, who was a US Army psychiatrist, was meant to treat soldiers for mental illness and other problems and "took them at their most vulnerable and gunned down these people where they lived". The announcement about a possible livestream has been met with criticism from both political parties. Republican Senator John Curtis pointed to Rome's history of a "bloody spectacle" corrupting people who watched them, warning that public executions erode civilisations "when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment". Curtis said that Hegseth's plan "risks feeding that appetite" and urged him to reconsider. "The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent," he said. Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN that the idea was "disgusting" and reminiscent of executions carried out by the Islamic State group. Georgia lawmaker Austin Scott, a Republican, said that he "absolutely" supports the death sentence, but that live-streaming executions "is what jihadists do. America is better than that". John Bolton, a former national security adviser during the first Trump administration, told BBC's Radio 4 PM that he supports capital punishment, but that the livestream is "unnecessary" because there are provisions for interested parties to view the execution in person or to report on it. "I just think this is a mark by Secretary Hegseth doing something he thinks will please President Trump. That's the way he's been running the defence department. I think that's really not appropriate for a secretary of defence," Bolton said. The US Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the decision to publicly livestream Hasan's execution, expressing "shock and great sorrow" in a statement. The UN human rights office told AFP that livestreaming it would be "tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture". Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines. He later admitted in court that he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base. Military law requires that military execution be approved by the US president. It also requires appellate review, when a higher court inspects the decision and gives a final judgement on its legality to move forward. While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International. When Hegseth told reporters on Thursday about plans to ensure the public can watch the execution, he did not specify where or how live video of the execution would be shown. A Pentagon spokesperson on Friday reiterated to the BBC that Hasan's execution "will be livestreamed," but said the government had no further details "to provide at this time". The White House did not respond to an inquiry about whether it expected to show Hasan's planned execution on its social media channels. The White House maintains official accounts and channels on the most notable and widely used online platforms that are capable of streaming live video, namely Meta, YouTube, TikTok and X. All of the platforms have prohibitions in place on violent images and videos, as well as those that show death or glorify or make a spectacle of violence. Meta, owner of Instagram, Facebook and Threads, explicitly bans any live stream of capital punishment. YouTube bans all "violent or gory content intended to shock or disgust viewers". TikTok has a similar rule that bars "extremely graphic, violent, or disturbing content—especially when it could cause viewers emotional distress." That includes the "moment of someone's death" and "the shooting of an individual". Both YouTube and TikTok make exceptions in instances of "public interest". Asked if a live-stream of an execution qualifies for the exception if it is government-sanctioned , a TikTok spokeswoman said: "Regardless, I'd point you back to the not allowed section which reflects our approach." The policy at X, which has loosened content moderation since billionaire Elon Musk took over the platform, prohibits content "glorifying" of violence. It will remove content depicting when a person dies will be removed if requested by certain parties. Meta, YouTube and X did not respond to multiple BBC requests for comment on whether they would uphold their current policies in the event Hasan's execution is broadcast. Rules on the recording and filming of executions differ between state, federal and military regulations. Pete Hegseth says the execution will be public, but a legal expert says the "unprecedented" decision is on "uncertain legal terrain". Alonzo Lunsford tells the BBC the punishment befits the crime but he has some doubts whether the public should be able to watch it. title: Watch: Who is Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay?
content: Navi Pillay, a former International Criminal Court judge and United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. In a statement announcing the award, the Nobel Committee praised Pillay's "efforts to promote peace and international law". BBC correspondent Joe Inwood explains how Pillay's childhood in South Africa led her to become a driving force in international law and human rights, from Rwanda to Gaza. Read more about this story. Swedish driver Susanne Callin has won the European Top Fuel championship for the second year in a row. Is drag racing the first gender-equal sport? He was arrested in Russia in 2023 and later sentenced to 16 years on espionage charges. Xi’s first visit to Washington in a decade was a display of pomp and pageantry, with Trump offering his guest a two-month truce on the brewing tariff war. title: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
content: As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets. "There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school. "We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen." He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds. Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down. "They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population." The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis. The protests - ignited at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in the deprived Paris suburb of Créteil - have struck a chord across the country. Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycées soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter. The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system. The problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them. On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million. But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them. Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem. It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages. When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils). "It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains. On Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget. But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country. "It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycée student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la République, a place synonymous with protest. "It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future." The unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries. So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry. More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks. But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers. A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens. Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade. A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth. "For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether." Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests. But Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests. "These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers and they run. This is not the message we want to send to the world." Police chiefs say violence, directed by agitators who have no link to the schools, is making their job incredibly hard. Michel Chaballier, deputy secretary-general of the National Police Commissioners' Union (SCPN), says he fears the "political climate has been radicalised", and it was more and more difficult to have a calm, constructive public debate ahead of the national vote next spring. "Police officers find themselves caught in the middle of this social tension, which is sometimes fuelled by irresponsible politicians," he says. "That's a shame, because I think this country deserves better." The protests have become another bruising battleground in France's culture wars, with leaders of the hard left and right seeking to capitalise. More than three-quarters of under-30s in France interviewed for an Ipsos survey conducted for Aix-Marseille University this week said they were worried about the state of their country. But many people have a more profound and wider concern about just how dramatically the middle ground in France is eroding, leaving a chasm in the political landscape. The education crisis is symptomatic of this but also threatens to act as an accelerant. Most polling suggests more and more French citizens are looking to political extremes for answers to their problems – whether they are linked to education, the economy, identity or immigration. Marine Le Pen of the hard right National Rally is the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race. Next, neck and neck, are Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Philippe was a prime minister in President Emmanuel Macron's first term and has since founded a centre-right party called Horizons. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a veteran hard-left politician and founder of France Unbowed (LFI), has been a prominent older face among the students at rallies over the past three weeks. Opponents have accused him of provoking and profiting from the unrest, while he counters that only his party truly represents the French youth. He claims the current movement that has emerged from the schools protest is the most potent since 1968, when huge demonstrations almost brought down the government of President Charles de Gaulle. At its height, 10 million workers were on the streets before fresh elections led to the revolt fizzling out, but not before carving an indelible memory in French social history. Despite being born more than four decades later, an exasperated generation of French teenagers are looking to the past for inspiration. "I personally want to reproduce 1968!" Massicella declares in Lille, as she nears the end of the protest march. Le Pen has stayed away from the protests and her most notable interventions have come in condemning the damage to schools, which is said to run into the millions of euros. She has also suggested that parents of children who have committed the vandalism should pay for repairs. The principle of casseur-payeur – those who break have to pay – has been an impassioned topic that has dominated French media this week. The problem for President Macron is that there is no quick fix. This is not a scenario where there is an unpopular piece of legislation that can be withdrawn in a hasty reverse ferret the prime minister is tasked with performing. That was the case with the gilets jaunes – the relentless protest in high vis jackets over a fuel tax rise nearly a decade ago. Wholesale reform of the education system would cost billions – in new classrooms, new facilities, new teachers – and take years to achieve. And changes that may seem more easily done – such as a reduction of the length of the school day – would be hugely problematic to implement logistically. What is more, any proposals which appease the students and end the current protests would have to be agreed at a time when France's finances are in a mess. The cost of servicing the national debt each year has now exceeded the core state education budget. Under the 2027 draft budget, there will be a 1.7% rise in education spending - but this is an under-inflation increase. Le Pen has vowed to cut public spending even further if she enters the Élysée Palace. She is banking that her promises to cut debt, curb migration and restrict certain benefits to French citizens will eclipse any criticism over her position on the protesting pupils. For her, discipline, a traditional curriculum and pride in France's history should be the defining features of every classroom. But many students are showing little sign of backing down from another French tradition. "In France, we have this tradition and history of revolting," says Alcidor in Paris. "That's the way we gained our rights and the way we will always gain them. That's our spirit." As the rain came outside the Lycée Voltaire central in Paris this week, the reality of having been up early once again to block the main gate started to kick in and the energy of the crowd dipped. But not for long. A huge cheer erupted as a senior teacher unlocked the hulking front door and poked her head out into the street. "The canteen is still open." The hunger for better schools among France's youth and better days for everyone else will not be so easily sated. title: Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
content: A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified. The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October. That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak. More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date. Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus. The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell. The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business. Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati. The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there. His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home. Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September. Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection. Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria. On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care. We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases. However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town. Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease. But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day. Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May. The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August. But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police. It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border. Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October. Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations. Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks. Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital. By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding. Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo. He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures. The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues. The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital. Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials. Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later. Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival. "When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said. The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected. The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist. title: Ashe was too scared to cancel her wedding - the story became a hit song
content: No songwriter is ever off duty. And for the US pop singer Ashe, that included her wedding day. Last October, she was getting ready to tie the knot at a gorgeous hilltop ceremony in Nashville when inspiration struck. As she watched her family gather, the musician flashed back to her first wedding, almost a decade earlier. The contrast was stark. She's called that first marriage "horrifying". Her ex, who she met in college, was, she says, emotionally manipulative and psychologically abusive. He had insisted on a beachfront wedding, which sounds romantic until you learn that Ashe has a fear of the ocean. In the run-up, she had been tempted to call it off, but felt powerless to stand up for herself. On her second wedding day, she realised the opposite was true. "I'm in a happy, healthy relationship and I have total autonomy over my own life," says the singer, now in her early 30s. "I thought, if this didn't feel right, I could totally put a halt to the whole thing. I definitely didn't have that first time around." As she adjusted her veil and prepared to walk down the aisle, she filed that feeling away. Two months later, and back at work, the idea resurfaced and a song spilled out. Its name? Stop the Wedding. It unfolds like a movie scene. Ashe pleads with her younger self to trust her instincts. "You know how you really feel / You don't have to waste your life," she sings, as the wedding band stutters to an uncertain halt. "Do I wish I'd had that advice at the time? 1,000 per cent," Ashe says. "If someone had given me the insight that I was not stuck, and that I could run, I could have changed things sooner. Maybe not at the altar. Maybe weeks before – but it was something I really could have used." What about the line where she pledges to "burn the wedding dress and run away"? "I didn't burn my dress," she laughs, "but I did get into a bathtub with it for a photoshoot right after I left my ex-husband, which really ruined it!" Released in August, Stop The Wedding this week became one of the 10 most-played songs in the world on Spotify. On Friday, it broke into the top five of the UK singles chart, while on TikTok, thousands of videos use Ashe's song to highlight red flags in their own relationships. "I don't think I even let myself dream of this," she says of the song's popularity. "It's something you hope for when you're first starting out, but when you've been in the business for 10 years, it's a little bit of a shock to the system." The success is even sweeter because, three years ago, Ashe nearly quit music altogether. A native of San Jose, she grew up in a conservative household where the radio was permanently tuned to Christian stations. It was her grandad who introduced her to rock music, playing Tom Petty and Bob Dylan on long road trips. By her teens, she was writing her own music. After studying orchestral composition at Boston's Berklee College of Music, she moved to Nashville and quickly found work as a songwriter. She scored an early credit on Demi Lovato's 2017 song You Don't Do It For Me Anymore; but slowly grew frustrated that other people were singing her words. The decision to become Ashe, whose full name is Ashlyn Rae Willson, didn't happen overnight. She appeared as a featured vocalist on a handful of dance tracks before plunging into a solo career. Her then-husband was not impressed. "I remember him saying, '[After this] no-one's ever going to love you for you. Anyone you meet now is going to meet you as Ashe, and I met you before'. "It was truly manipulative, and it kept me stuck. It kept me stuck for a long, long time." It can't be a coincidence that a song she wrote after signing her divorce papers became her breakthrough hit. Moral of The Story (key lyric: " you can think that you're in love / when you're really just in pain ") was released in 2019, and hit one billion streams after appearing in the hit Netflix series To All the Boys: PS I Still Love You. Ashe was suddenly playing bigger venues and duetting with Niall Horan, but work became all consuming. When her brother died of an overdose in 2020, she was back on stage within a month. "There was so much momentum and I was saying yes to far too many things," she reflects now. "It got to a point where the idea of touring was giving me panic attacks, and I just couldn't stomach being Ashe, which is such a shame, because I'm her." In 2023, she had a nervous breakdown and stepped away from showbusiness. "I had to halt everything. I bought a house in Nashville, I gardened, I saw a therapist and I gave myself a chance to miss music." For six months, she led a quiet, domestic life. But when pop singer Suki Waterhouse invited her to a session, it rekindled her passion for writing. She made a tentative return with 2024's deeply confessional album Wilson, then teamed up with Billie Eilish's brother Finneas O'Connell to form The Favors, before signing a new deal with Atlantic Records. Those experiences mean she's treating the success of Stop The Wedding very differently. "You can get swept up by all the updates on your phone, but this time I'm navigating the emotions of that, and also going for a four-mile walk and calling my mom. "There's a real groundedness." The same can't be said for her new album, Girl of Your Dreams, which is almost deliriously over the top. Stop The Wedding sets the tone, with abrupt tempo changes that track Ashe's inner turmoil. Lasso The Moon is more whimsical, setting out the star's outlandish requirements for a new partner. "God forbid I raise my standards," she laughs. Love Bomb explores the psychology of a manipulative ex (guess who?); while Swan Lake is a comically villainous portrait of Ashe's possessiveness, complete with a Bugsy Malone chorus line. It's a deliberately maximalist record, recalling the lush orchestrations of ELO and The Carpenters, with a nod to the revivalist pop of Ashe's friend Laufey. "We were so bored of making music that's boring," she says. "It scratches an itch for me as an artist to do something different and not meet the status quo." The album ends back at her second wedding. The closing track focuses on the "real, true, constant love" she's found with musician John Clark Canada. "You'll be my Tuesday night and my Sunday drive / And the last speech at my funeral," she sings. Expanding on that idea, Ashe incorporates the ebullient sound of a New Orleans funeral band in the song's closing moments. And the person they're burying is the disillusioned girl from Stop The Wedding. Ashe's album, Girl of Your Dreams, is out on 16 October. title: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
content: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans. The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order. The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially. However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar". The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC and said they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions. They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims. The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and counts 125 countries as member states. Several major countries remain outside the ICC, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel. The Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted. But Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC." The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software. Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution. He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories, including the UK, to "rein in" the institution. The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function. Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty". The ICC said that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred". It called the measures "an assault on the rule of law" and said no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice, adding: "History will judge this moment." This showdown potentially marks the gravest crisis in the court's 24-year history. Rather than targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, the US is now sanctioning the court itself. The sanctions could ultimately see the ICC unable to try cases, meaning detainees awaiting trial or judgment could have to be released, according to Professor Ryan Goodman from the New York University School of Law. Among those awaiting trial in The Hague is Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines. The 81-year-old is accused of the extrajudicial killing of thousands during his deadly "war on drugs" between 2011 and 2019. Others awaiting trial or with pending appeals include former senior figures accused of war crimes in Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic. Goodman says that as a senator, Rubio was "out front" highlighting Duterte's alleged crimes. He told the BBC such a release would be "enormously damaging to the global effort towards international justice [and] towards the Philippines". "[For] the victims, it just has to be incredibly traumatic because a lot of them participate in the ICC proceedings to put themselves on the line with a hope that justice will come around," adds Goodman, a former special counsel at the US Department of Defence. Among the carve-outs announced as part of today's sanctions are "licenses" allowing the ICC to continue "services for the operation of facilities used for the detention" of Duterte and others. However, Goodman says ultimately these detainees may have to be released "as a matter of law" if the financial sanctions mean the court cannot conduct fair trials or appeals. The planned firing-squad execution on 3 December has led to questions about legality and purpose. Police say they checked the concert venue in Tulsa, Oklahoma but "could not find any threat". The storm took direct aim at Florida and is expected to impact Alabama, Georgia, and Louisiana. The bodies of Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend Carter Rhoad were found at the bottom of a well. The planned execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad would be the first military execution in more than 60 years. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Two Renoir paintings stolen from French museum are recovered
content: Two paintings by Auguste Renoir stolen a month ago from a museum in the south of France have been recovered, the local town hall has said. The two works were seized on 8 September when thieves cut through a fence and smashed a window at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, where the French impressionist had lived during his final years. The local mayor praised authorities for recovering the paintings and said the news gave immense joy and profound relief. Six suspects have also been arrested in relation with the heist at Renoir Museum, the town hall confirmed in a statement. The theft was the latest in a series of high-profile art heists in Europe. The two missing paintings were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886). The thieves had used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings inside the museum and had initially made off with four paintings, but dropped two of them in the museum's garden as they fled "These two paintings are far more than works of art. They are part of our city's history, our cultural heritage and the legacy Auguste Renoir left to Cagnes-sur-Mer," said Mayor Bryan Masson, who is part of France's National Rally. The town hall said initially that it would provide further details of the recovery on Friday, but cancelled a planned press conference. The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks. Opened in 1960, it houses a variety of objects that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters. Earlier this year paintings by Renoir, Paul Cézanne and Henri Matisse were stolen from a museum near the Italian city of Parma, in a raid that lasted just three minutes. They were recovered in August. France saw its biggest art robbery in years last October, when crown jewels were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris. Disguised as construction workers, the thieves broke into the Louvre's first-floor Apollo Gallery during the museum's opening hours. They used an angle-grinder to open display cases and made off with €88m (£78m) of jewels that once belonged to France's 19th-Century queens and empresses. The Louvre was subsequently criticised for under-investing in security. Students taking to the streets in France have become a focal point in the country's increasingly polarised politics. Education minister Edouard Geffray makes the offer after another day of sometimes violent demonstrations by high-school students. Jose Mourinho defends Kylian Mbappe who has been scrutinised during the international break. Shire Hall has been opened in 2019 but the trust says it can no longer afford to keep it open. title: Three Saudi nationals killed in Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport
content: Three Saudi Arabian nationals have been killed in two attacks on the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, the country's civil aviation authority has said, after Yemen's Houthis said they had targeted the facility. The attacks also resulted in "injuries to a number of Saudi citizens and residents of various nationalities", the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement on X. It added that the first attack on Thursday targeted the airport while the second had struck an aircraft belonging to state carrier Saudia. One of its pilots was among those killed, the airline said in a statement. Air traffic had returned to normal, the civil aviation authority said. Yemen's Houthi group said on Thursday it had attacked the airport with two ballistic missiles. The Iran-aligned group said it had also targeted an airport in Najran city near the Saudi border with Yemen, and Khamis Mushait air base further north. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed these attacks. The latest casualties follow the deaths of three people in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on 6 and 7 October. Two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, the civil aviation body said on Wednesday. Another person was killed at King Khalid airport in Riyadh. The latest attacks come amid a marked escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west. The Houthi military spokesman said the previous two attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports were in "response to the Saudi aggression against our country" that saw "60 air strikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours". The group says it is targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war. The conflict has worsened in recent weeks, after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive. That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping. But Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea. A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government. A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. But the informal ceasefire began to unravel in July. The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating against what they say is a years-long Saudi blockade and for an air strike on Sanaa airport. The families allege that men with links to the Saudi government helped those who carried out the 2001 attacks, something the country denies. In rare access to Taiz, the BBC World Service speaks to children, teachers and families affected by the war. Anojan Sivarasa faces execution after he was found guilty of blasphemy over a Facebook comment. The Yemeni president's announcement comes amid an exchange of strikes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition. Experts say US military assistance, using shuttle tankers and pipelines bypassing the Strait of Hormuz mean exports have rebounded. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Thai Queen makes first solo flight in fighter jet
content: Thailand's Queen Suthida made her first solo flight in a fighter jet, according to the Thai Royal Household. The Queen was shown boarding a Gripen on 8 October at an airfield in Surat Thani province, southern Thailand, while King Maha Vajiralongkorn watched from the ground. The Royal Household has said she is an experienced pilot, having logged about 1,188 hours across several types of aircraft since she began flying in 2010. She also co-piloted aircraft carrying the King on official visits to other countries, the Royal Household said. We explain why Indonesia’s peatland fires are so difficult to battle and produce so much haze. The BBC’s Tessa Wong breaks down how one of Indonesia’s worst wildfire seasons is impacting countries around South East Asia. Police have said it is “strongly suspected” that the incident was caused by a gas leak. Indonesian lawmakers on Wednesday ordered the demolition of a controversial luxury compound inside a penitentiary near the capital. The municipality building in Baglung was left teetering on an unstable ledge due to floods before it fell into a river. A surprise inspection at the prison revealed apartment-like units appearing to house inmates, equipped with televisions, a gym and fridges stocked with alcohol. BBC correspondent Azadeh Moshiri reports from Delhi, where hundreds of women are protesting. Around 175,000 people in Indonesia have suffered from respiratory illness since August. The BBC is in Inner Mongolia where dozen of Chinese data centres are being constructed, as the country aims to lead the world in artificial intelligence. Lian Yunzhi broke the women's world record twice in three days at World Cube Association competitions. The typhoon is passing Japan's eastern coast, bringing major disruption and heavy rainfall in its wake. Verified footage appears to show a cargo ship colliding with a fishing boat near Singapore, with investigators still working to establish exactly when and how the crash happened. BBC Eye has discovered a teacher who was imprisoned for sexually assaulting a student in Indonesia has been secretly released early. The BBC goes inside a fortified storage facility to view luxury goods seized by police that are now up for auction. Rescuers are searching for survivors after the vessel travelling from the mainland to a popular tourist destination caught fire. Emergency teams were still searching for at least 86 missing people in the waters off the coast of Coron, in the Philippines. Chandika Shrestha was airlifted to hospital after spending more than 10 days in her partially buried house. There are still hundreds of workers trapped in a network of tunnels that run along the Trishuli river. Rescuers pull two people from a hydropower tunnel more than a week after a massive flash flood devastated the Nepal-China border. title: Can the Fort Hood shooter's execution be livestreamed?
content: The US Department of Defense says they plan to livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood military base in 2009. It is believed it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. But can the US military actually livestream an execution? Rules on the recording and filming of executions differ between state, federal and military regulations - as Aisha Sembhi explains. Design by Mark Edwards. The US aircraft carrier was set to return in May but the war with Iran has kept it at sea on one of the longest deployments ever. BBC Verify used ship-tracking websites to follow UK and French vessels which monitored the migrant boat in the English Channel. BBC Verify looks at footage showing the aftermath of a strike on a building in southern Iran. A small boat has crossed the English Channel carrying 230 people. BBC Verify looks into whether the boats are getting bigger. Pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England will be given a 20% cut to business rates, funded by a review of tax relief on businesses like vape shops. BBC Verify debunks Trump's claim of a "suspect" referee following Folarin Balogun's World Cup red card. The education, health and welfare systems are no longer fit for purpose in preparing young people for adult life, a new report says. AI-generated images from the Met Gala have spread on social media - we explain how to spot the fakes. BBC Verify has been looking into whether the US blockade of Iran near the Strait of Hormuz is working. The BBC's Analysis Editor Ros Atkins looks at the questions around the way Buckingham Palace has responded to the various accusations against the King's brother. Revelations over Peter Mandelson’s links to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein have raised questions about how he became ambassador. Our Analysis Editor Ros Atkins reports. Two years after the 7 October attacks, dozens of hostages remain in Hamas captivity. BBC Verify has been examining what we know about them. The BBC's analysis editor looks at a decision that leading Democrats have called "an abuse of power". Using footage and flight data, BBC Verify has pieced together what we know so far about the Air India crash in Ahmedabad. The IDF have released new footage that they say shows the underground tunnel network underneath the European hospital in southern Gaza. BBC Verify pieces together the evidence. BBC Analysis Editor Ros Atkins and the BBC Verify team build up a picture of what happened and how it was done. The UN Human Rights Office has said it believes 47 people were injured in Gaza on Tuesday when crowds overwhelmed an aid distribution centre run by a controversial US and Israeli-backed group. BBC Verify analysed footage, gathered witness testimony and spoke to munitions and legal experts to examine how one of Gaza's last functioning hospitals came under Israeli attack. CCTV footage obtained and verified by the BBC shows the moment before impact and the immediate aftermath. Munitions experts told BBC Verify that the strikes and destruction are consistent with the use of so-called "bunker buster" bombs - designed to hit underground targets. BBC Verify's Merlyn Thomas has more. As Ukraine reckons with the terms of a possible peace deal, BBC Verify asks what it could mean in practice. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved.
