title: We sold everything and bought a one-way ticket to take our three children travelling
content: Dani and Tom Wooldridge worked hard to transform a 1970s house into a beloved family home after they bought it about seven years ago. Dani, 39, a nurse, also ran an aesthetics business while Tom, 38, had a construction business. Three children, a close extended family and lots of friends. A happy life. Yet in May this year, the five of them sold their possessions and home and bought a one-way ticket heading for Indonesia, with the only things they owned in the world now stowed in backpacks in the luggage compartment. With Olivia, 12, Morgan, seven, and four-year-old George, the Woolridges are planning to travel the world, with no endpoint in sight, hoping to see every continent. Five months in, over a video call from the Indonesian island of Lombok, Dani and Tom explain the decisions which have brought them to the shores of south-east Asia. Both of them had gone travelling for a period of time in their early 20s, a classic gap-year style experience, and had enjoyed taking holidays, particularly to sunny destinations. Dani says: "It was always a conversation we had but once you start having kids and you've got the mortgage and everything like that it's kind of, oh it's not the right time." But nearly two years ago, the family took a holiday to Thailand over Christmas. "We were fortunate enough to have a month over there, travelled round with the kids and obviously they were almost two years younger than they are now, and managed really well. "It all went really smoothly and it was great seeing the kids experience a completely different world to what we'd all grown up. It just felt so great exploring with them," Tom added. Dani says that sparked their interest to start researching and meeting other families who had decided to jet off. "We made lots of lists – lots of positives, lots of negatives," she says. "Can we do this? How are we still going to educate our children? We had a home, we had our businesses, we had careers. What do we do about all that?" Once they made the decision, they knew they had to be "100% committed". Dani thought at first they should rent their house out "so we've got something to come back to" but Tom wanted to sell, and the couple realised they didn't want to leave the responsibility of managing it to people back home. The boys were excited about the idea from the start but the couple admit it was harder for their daughter. Tom says: "Olivia was a bit nervous. She'd just started high school in the September and we left in May this year. She was very apprehensive about leaving all her friends. "Morgan and George do mention their friends now and again but they're a bit younger so they didn't have that emotional attachment as much as Olivia." When they told their parents about their plans, their initial reaction was "why are you selling everything you've worked so hard to get?" "Most people have got bets on when we're coming back," Dani says, laughing. Tom adds: "They've all got a year each." After selling their house at the start of the year, they lived in rented accommodation for a number of months, before heading to the airport in May for the big farewell. Leaving was "very emotional", Dani says. "We were very fortunate that we had a lot of family coming to the airport with us," adds Tom. "We'd checked our luggage in, and we got to the security gates, and that was hard. "We were so fortunate to have a close family and friendship group as well. They're the people we miss and that's what we miss from back home, the people that were in our lives. Not so much the material things we had." However once the plane had taken off and the goodbyes were behind them, the excitement started to kick in. "We remembered where we were going," joked Tom. But even though they had both been to their first destination, Bali in Indonesia, before, the culture shock still hit them. "It's just everything. Your senses are just heightened. It's the smells, seeing everything around, it's so different to home. "We went to Bali 15 years ago when it was a lot quieter," adds Dani. "People have said how busy it is now, and it was. The first day or two was very overwhelming. Our daughter was still a bit emotional. She was up and down with things and we were all a bit jet lagged. "We went to Uluwatu first and it has got so busy. Even us walking down a road, I was nervous. Scooters everywhere." But there were also upsides, Tom says. "The food instantly was amazing. And the people are just beautiful, and so kind. And just to feel the heat on our skin." They moved to different parts of the island, swapping the beaches in the south to climb the volcanic Mount Batur in the north, and spending time in the cultural village of Ubud inland. They then went island hopping eastwards across the Indonesian archipelago before doubling back to Lombok for a second stay. "We were moving around quite a bit," Dani says. "So each time it was almost like that feeling of going home because we were packing up, but we weren't going home. I think it took us months to really think, wow, we're not actually going home." Leaving the UK behind has not meant abandoning education, Dani stresses. "Even though we want our children to experience the world and have that kind of real world learning, we have said we also want them to have opportunities. So if they want to go to university and be a doctor or a nurse or whatever career path they want to go down, we still want them to have those opportunities," she says. They have a "huge bag" full of textbooks and workbooks recommended by teachers before they left and they are following the UK teaching curriculum. Olivia has an online maths tutor, who was previously head of maths at her high school in Rhondda Cynon Taf, and had also taught Tom at the same school. The boys have a tutor who covers the primary curriculum with them and does English and some science with Olivia. Although the big downside to their journey is missing time with family back home, Dani and Tom say the cultural experiences and confidence the children have already gained from their travels, meeting such a wide variety of people and having the opportunity to live such an outdoor life, outweighs the negatives. The family is due to be moving on to Malaysia after spending five months travelling around Indonesia, most recently in Lombok for a second stint, where the children have been attending a world schooling centre which the couple described as a "lovely routine" with amazing friends. After bringing "way too much stuff" with them initially, they have given away possessions to locals they have met along their travels and refined it down to two large 120-litre backpacks for the parents and two 100-litre rolling packs including one filled with educational materials. "The kids will have virtually nothing on their backs, just maybe a really small backpack to get on the plane," says Tom. "We thought the kids would be excited at carrying their backpacks. Yeah, they're not onboard with that," laughs Dani. Among the things they have planned for Malaysia is visiting an orangutang sanctuary in Borneo and another longer stop at a world-schooling centre to give the children more chances to spend time with peers. Then they move into Thailand, where both Dani's mum and Tom's parents will make separate visits and after figuring out a good location to celebrate Dani's 40th birthday, will move through Cambodia, Vietnam and the Philippines. With all that, they have the next year "roughly" planned out. They have allowed for contingencies and emergencies – Tom has already had to fly home once for a funeral – but don't have a firm destination in mind yet once they leave Asia, barring a likely brief visit home to catch up with family. "We're going to do as much as we feel we want to in a continent and then go to the next one," explains Tom. "Just keep going for as long as we can, and want to. If at some point we don't want to then we'll have explored a lot of places to pick somewhere to stop." It is, in many respects, the bucket list to end all bucket lists. But if they had to put one destination at the top, what would it be? For Dani, it's to go on an African safari. "I've always wanted to see Africa and I've never been. That's always been on my list." Tom says: "Tahiti is coming to my head. That's with my surfing background. The place looks beautiful. And we will be going there. I'm 40 next December so..." title: Epstein floods the midterms as campaigns spend $35 million on more than 160 ads
content: Jeffrey Epstein has been dead for seven years, but he’s all over campaign ads this election season, invoked overwhelmingly by Democrats — and occasionally by Republicans — to attack opponents or promote themselves. A CNN analysis found that candidates and outside groups have aired more than 160 unique Epstein-related ads in the 2026 midterms, backed by more than $35 million in airtime. That marks a striking jump from the 2024 presidential election, when only three such ads aired — all in local Florida races, where the Epstein scandal first erupted. President Donald Trump and his allies helped keep the issue alive during the 2024 campaign by promising greater transparency and raising expectations that more Epstein records would be released. But this year, Democrats are driving the advertising surge, accounting for nearly 90% of the ads identified by CNN this cycle. The ads underscore the political potency of the Epstein saga, nearly a year after the Justice Department released millions of pages of files following a bruising political fight led mostly by Democrats in Congress. While public pressure for accountability has been building for years, the issue hasn’t featured prominently in elections – until this season. Polling from the spring shows majorities of voters from both political parties believed the Epstein files showed that powerful people are rarely held accountable for their actions, but it’s unclear how the issue is playing out in the midterm elections. Many of the attack ads feature misleading or even false claims about their opponents, including criticism over failing to vote for the release of the Epstein files, and, sometimes, tenuous ties to former Epstein associates or the so-called “Epstein class.” The bulk of Epstein ad spending has gone toward battleground Senate races, reflecting the intensity of the messaging efforts there. Contests in Georgia, Texas and Ohio rank as the top three in terms of money spent on Epstein-related ads, with much of that money coming from well-funded Democrats making the controversy a point of emphasis in their campaigns. In Georgia, more than $10 million has been spent on ads related to Epstein, according to data from Ad Impact, with more than three quarters of that money coming directly from the campaign of Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff. He has repeatedly attacked his opponent, Republican Rep. Mike Collins, casting Collins as a Trump loyalist who voted against releasing the Epstein files. “Mike Collins voted to cover up the Epstein files. Even after he knew 14-year-old girls had been raped,” said a former US marshal in one Ossoff Facebook ad . “He tried to tell us it was a hoax.” But that ad is misleading. Collins, along with all but nine House Republicans, voted against a procedural vote to release the files in July 2025, but he ultimately did vote for the release of the files in November of last year after Trump, reversing course, encouraged Republicans to vote for it. Collins also did not directly use the word “hoax,” but his team pointed to a Trump Truth Social post calling it the “Jeffrey Epstein Hoax” to deflect against a government shutdown. Collins, in turn, has accused Ossoff of hypocrisy for accepting campaign donations from tech billionaire Reid Hoffman, a liberal donor and former Epstein associate who once visited Epstein’s private island. (Hoffman has not been accused of any wrongdoing related to Epstein’s crimes and has expressed regret for his association with Epstein.) Collins then challenged Ossoff to return the money. And in Ohio, more than $6 million has been spent on Epstein ads. Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost the seat in 2024, and Republican Sen. Jon Husted have both bent the truth to attack the other over campaign donations from “associates” of Epstein. Brown has launched ad after ad attempting to tie Husted to Les Wexner, the Ohio-based billionaire and former Victoria’s Secret CEO who once employed Epstein as his money manager. The Epstein files indicated Wexner was at one time considered a potential co-conspirator to Epstein’s crimes by the FBI. “Husted’s taken over $116,000 from one of Epstein’s closest friends and co-conspirators, and last year took a maximum donation from him just weeks before voting to block the release of the Epstein files. Jon Husted: Who’s he really working for?” the narrator of one anti-Husted ad read . Wexner, who has denied any allegations of wrongdoing related to Epstein, contributed to Husted over a 20-year period. Husted also accepted a donation from Wexner as recently as the summer of 2025. Husted voted against a release of the files by the attorney general in a procedural vote that September, though he later voted in November 2025 unanimously with the rest of the Senate to release the files after Trump, facing pressure, urged Republicans to vote in favor of it. A spokesperson for Husted, Amy Natoce, stated the campaign donated more than $34,000 to anti-sex trafficking charities from available funds. Previous funds donated from Wexner were already spent and no longer accessible. In turn, Husted responded with an ad of his own, calling Brown a liar: “Thirty-two years in DC made Sherrod Brown a liar. The truth: Jon Husted voted to release the Epstein files while Senator Brown took $100,000 from Epstein associates,” said the ad’s narrator. The Husted campaign provided CNN with a breakdown of those alleged Brown donors with ties to Epstein, including Hoffman and former Harvard president Larry Summers. But the list also includes donors who have tenuous connections to Epstein or whose connection predates Epstein’s mid-2000s arrest, such as billionaire philanthropist George Soros, hedge fund billionaire David E. Shaw and Hollywood agent Casey Wasserman. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico’s campaign has spent at least $4.9 million on ads regarding a plea deal Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton’s office made with an alleged child sex offender to serve just a total of one day in jail. The ad ’s narrator called the deal “an Epstein-style sweetheart deal for a well-connected child predator” before saying: “Ken Paxton’s corruption endangers our kids. We don’t need any more pedophile protectors in Washington.” Epstein cut a secret and unprecedented deal with federal prosecutors nearly two decades ago that allowed him to avoid federal sex trafficking charges and serve just 13 months in a county prison on state prostitution charges, including one that involved a minor. Epstein continued to abuse young girls and women even while he was on house arrest, according to survivors. Paxton’s office’s plea deal sparked outrage in the state earlier this year, even drawing a rebuke from the judge. The case initially resulted in a mistrial, leaving prosecutors to choose between retrying the case or agreeing to a plea deal with the offender. Testifying in court can often retraumatize victims, particularly minors, and the victim and their family declined to do so again. That led the prosecutors to forge a plea deal, one the victim’s family signed off on. Paxton defended the plea deal at a campaign event in late September. “It’s more important to make sure that this kid is protected than to get the verdict that we actually want. So, it’s so dishonest to present it any other way because that’s actually what happened,” he said. The victim’s family has said publicly they are “tired of being used in this election.” Epstein ads have recently flooded the airwaves in key Senate races in Iowa, Maine , Alaska and Kansas , too. In Colorado, the family of Virginia Giuffre, the most high-profile Epstein abuse survivor who died by suicide in 2025, appeared in an attack ad from Democrat Jessica Killin against Republican Rep. Jeff Crank, who represents the state’s 5th Congressional District. Giuffre’s brother and sister-in-law say that Crank refused to meet with them as his constituents and that he voted to cover up the Epstein files. “Virginia deserved better,” said Sky Roberts, Giuffre’s brother, addressing the camera. “Jeff Crank covered up Epstein’s crimes to protect Donald Trump.” Crank did not sign onto a bipartisan petition to release the Epstein files and voted to block its consideration on the House floor. But he ultimately voted in favor of releasing them last November after Trump urged such a vote. A spokesperson for Crank told CNN a Republican Congress released the files and called the ad’s claims “intentionally vague” and unsupported by the facts.” Some ads grossly distort a candidate’s ties to Epstein and indict anyone who has been mentioned in the files. Inclusion in the Epstein files does not inherently indicate wrongdoing. In Nebraska, Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts painted independent Dan Osborn in multiple ads as a money-hungry politician cashing in on campaign checks. One ad said that Osborn was “funded by members of the Epstein class” and criticized him for fundraising with an “alleged Epstein trafficker.” That ad name checks Dana Chasin, a Democratic operative whose name appears once within the files as part of a 2024 email in which a lawyer representing a woman said she had flown on Chasin’s “small prop plane” to Epstein’s New York home. The woman alleges she was later sexually abused by a billionaire investor associate of Epstein’s. Chasin denied the allegations, telling Politico in February that “nothing pertaining to me in the March 2024 email” was true and that he had never met Epstein, Maxwell or those named associates. CNN reached out to Chasin but did not receive a response. The Osborn campaign cancelled a fundraising event with Chasin in February and said it donated money Chasin contributed to an anti-sex trafficking nonprofit. Conservative outlet The Daily Wire later reported i t was still soliciting donations on the ActBlue platform for that event that month after the campaign shut it down. A spokesperson for Osborn’s campaign called it “laughable” to tie Osborn to Epstein. The Ricketts campaign responded by raising questions about when Osborn cancelled the fundraiser and whether they donated all of the money for that event. In early October, Osborn’s campaign launched an ad showing two degrees of separation between Epstein, Ricketts’ donors and Ricketts. “If you want a senator who takes money from Epstein’s circle, Pete Ricketts is your guy,” the ad narrator said. In New Hampshire, Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas has targeted Republican John E. Sununu, a former senator running once more, because “his name appears in the Epstein files and [he] denied ever attending an elite event in Doha, Qatar, that Jeffrey Epstein used for networking,” one Facebook ad from the Pappas campaign read . Sununu’s own campaign later acknowledged he did go to Doha in 2001 and attended the World Economic Forum event there in 2010, which was referenced in emails found within the Epstein files. In a 2010 email, Epstein name checks that “John Sununu” has “ good stories ” in an email referring to the event, but it is unclear which John Sununu — either the former senator or the former governor — Epstein was referring to. “As reported months ago, neither John nor his father ever met or communicated in any way with Boris Nikolich [sic] or Jeffrey Epstein. John believes Epstein was a despicable human being,” said campaign spokesperson Mike Schrimpf in a statement. And in New Mexico, an ad from the group Accountable New Mexico targeted gubernatorial Democratic nominee Deb Haaland, claiming she accepted a ride on “one of Epstein’s private jets to a DC fundraiser. She took tens of thousands of dollars from Epstein businesses, and the campaign even went back and asked for more.” Those claims are misleading, according to local media . In 2014, while Haaland was running as lieutenant governor on the Democratic ticket, she took a flight to DC for a fundraiser, but not on one of Epstein’s private planes. Epstein’s company commissioned the flight after her running mate, then-New Mexico Attorney General Gary King, requested it, according to an email in the files . It is unclear whether Haaland knew that at the time. The ad misrepresents an email sent to Epstein thanking him for his support, making it appear it was from Haaland. That email was from King. The ad also claimed Haaland accepted thousands of dollars in campaign donations from Epstein’s companies. However, in New Mexico, candidates for governor and lieutenant governor — despite later running on the same ticket — run separate campaign committees through the general election. King accepted Epstein campaign donations. Haaland released an ad of her own refuting the attack ad: “Fact checkers say Sam Bregman’s attacks against Deb Haaland are lies. Deb Haaland never flew on Jeffrey Epstein’s plane, never asked him for money, and supports a full investigation into his crimes,” a narrator said. Not all of the ads regarding Epstein are attack ads, however. Some candidates are positioning themselves against the so-called “Epstein class,” a term first coined by California Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna, that has since become a succinct anti-establishment cry for Democrats as they seek to reclaim power this fall. Ohio Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur, who faces another tight race for re-election, released an ad highlighting her vote to release the files: “I voted repeatedly to release every word and photo in the Epstein files, and I won’t let it go until they go to prison,” said Kaptur in the ad. “I don’t work for the ‘Epstein class’ — the selfish people that are selling us out. I work for you.” Rep. Jamie Raskin, a top House Democrat, fundraised against the “Epstein class, the Mar-a-Lago elite” in a Facebook ad that launched in March. Similarly, House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia has launched ads on Facebook this year to fundraise based off his work on the committee. Even in longshot House races against Republican leadership candidates are campaigning on the Epstein files. Conrad Cable, a former English major turned vegetable farmer running in Louisiana’s 4th Congressional District, has launched a handful of ads on Facebook accusing House Speaker Mike Johnson of orchestrating a cover up over the files. As has Lauren Jewett, a Democrat running in Louisiana’s 1st Congressional District against Rep. Steve Scalise, who holds the number two spot in House Republican Leadership. Self-styled Republican outsiders have also embraced this messaging. Paul Bondar, who unsuccessfully ran in Texas’ 32nd District congressional primary this spring, released an ad expressing his disgust with “the politicians stonewalling the Epstein files and not protecting kids.” For Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie, who played a key role in forcing a vote on the release of the Epstein files, the issue became all-encompassing. His campaign touted his efforts in campaign ads. “I’m demanding and leading the charge to ensure the Epstein files, which we were promised would be released, actually are in full,” Massie said in one spot . But that wasn’t enough to blunt a determined push by Trump and his allies to oust the iconoclastic conservative, as Massie lost in the primary to challenger Ed Gallrein after being targeted by more than $15 million in outside spending. CNN’s Casey Tolan contributed to this story.

title: Trump thinks he should have won the Nobel Peace Prize. His quest for it is now the butt of the joke
content: President Donald Trump is enduring his second straight Nobel loss. “The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t,” he said at a rally in Syracuse, New York, late Friday night, devoting a remarkable amount of time to discussing the prize that was awarded earlier in the day to South African human rights pioneer Navi Pillay . The president called it an “indelible stain on the country of Norway” and said he’d never heard of this year’s winner. (The prize is not awarded by the Norwegian government.) But Trump’s quixotic quest for his own Nobel — which included effectively coercing last year’s winner to give him her medal earlier this year— was the butt of a joke for the latest winner on Friday. “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump ,” Pillay quipped to an applauding crowd. The indignity for Trump caps what is now clearly a lost cause. But his campaign for the Nobel epitomizes the problems of his second term: He seeks personal glory, but he’s all too eager to try and take shortcuts to get there. And strewn along the path are haphazard and often counterproductive gambits. To recap: But the whole charade really fell apart early this year. That’s when Trump ramped up his talk about taking over Greenland. He even left open the possibility of taking it by force — effectively threatening an invasion of a NATO ally (although he later backed off that effort). He actually did invade Venezuela to arrest Nicolás Maduro. The White House might argue this was a humanitarian mission to free the Venezuelan people of an evil, criminal dictator. But Trump left the rest of the regime in power and has since pitched the invasion as an effective seizure of Venezuelan resources (read: oil). He even summarized the operation thusly last month at the United Nations General Assembly: “ To the victor belong the spoils .” That is not a phrase associated with the average Nobel Peace Prize winner. And he repeated it Friday night, adding, “We’re taking out for ourselves — we deserve it.” A couple weeks after the invasion, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado gave him her medal , apparently hoping it would convince Trump to more strongly support her cause. It has not worked. And then Trump in February launched a war against Iran, based on inconsistent and highly suspect claims , that has much of the world crying foul. The war, which has now stretched more than seven months, almost certainly eliminated any hope Trump had of winning a Nobel. That’s really the story here: Trump looking for his Nobel in all the wrong places — and constantly shooting himself in the foot in the process. If the president wanted a Nobel prize, it might have behooved him to try and hue a more closely to international law and not kill people who aren’t part of an armed conflict on the high seas. He might also not want to spend time cracking down on the opposition within the US while threatening and launching foreign invasions. And after failing to end a Russia-Ukraine war that he assured he could end on Day One of his presidency, Trump instead repeatedly exaggerated his role in ending wars. (And in some cases, they weren’t even actual wars.) Then, when he didn’t win the Nobel last year, he got other people to give him consolation prizes – even though, in both instances, the scene only seemed to drive home Trump’s desperation. Of course, he doesn’t seem all that worried about looking desperate. Just look at his long-running quest to put his name on things like the Kennedy Center . He seems focused on crafting the appearance of glory without the hard work and discipline. He’ll throw his weight around in hopes of winning laurels, even if the vast majority of other people don’t view them as legitimate or deserved. As recently as this week, Trump said it would be “ a great discredit to ” the Nobel Committee if he didn’t get the award. His attitude was summed up nicely in a New York Magazine interview last month. Reporter Ben Terris asked the president about Democratic Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff’s allegation that he is pursuing his own glorification because nobody else will build monuments to him when he’s gone. “ That’s true ,” Trump said. “Nobody will do it once I’m gone. When I leave here, nobody will.” This story has been updated with additional developments.

title: Inside Trump and Mamdani’s 2-hour phone call after the New York City ICE shooting
content: The friendly relationship between President Donald Trump and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani hit one of its toughest tests yet Thursday after a series of calls over a shooting involving immigration agents in the Bronx. Mamdani, who keeps an open line of communication with Trump, has argued that maintaining a working relationship with the president is a matter of pragmatism. Despite their stark ideological and political differences, Mamdani has suggested that direct engagement gives him a better chance of securing results for New Yorkers. On Thursday, Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents shot and wounded a man driving his car while his 5-year-old child was in the back seat during a targeted enforcement operation in the Bronx. The incident set up an opportunity for the mayor: Pressure Trump on an issue central to Democrats and a large swath of New Yorkers, try to get the victim released from federal custody and use the outcome to prove why his unlikely relationship with Trump is beneficial. In the end, the victim — a 28-year-old undocumented immigrant — remained in federal custody. Mamdani held multiple calls with the White House on Thursday night in what turned into an hourslong attempt to negotiate that the victim, Oscar Belgal, be released from custody. The Department of Homeland Security said Belgal has ties to the Trinitarios gang, a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny and prior arrests for assault, robbery, drug possession and weapons possession. As the hours passed, protesters descended on the neighborhood, getting into skirmishes with police. A person familiar with the talks described them as cordial in nature but said the two sides were extremely far apart in terms of what should happen next. A White House official confirmed the president had a lengthy conversation with Mamdani. Mamdani has maintained that his diplomatic approach to Trump has benefited New Yorkers, but Thursday’s shooting could strain his relationship with Trump and test just how much the mayor can actually leverage from it. At one point during the talks, Trump, Mamdani and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin tried to hash out a compromise that would allow the injured driver to be released from federal custody. Mullin and Trump were willing. But only if Belgal was transferred to the custody of the New York Police Department. The Dominican national suffered a superficial neck wound when officers opened fire as they approached his vehicle. Mullin said that during the call, Trump suggested to Mamdani the NYPD had enough reason to hold him given his criminal record, but the mayor refused. “He was wanting us to release this individual back onto the streets,” Mullin told reporters Friday. “If NYPD wants to take the charges and pursue the charges, we’ll be happy to release him into the custody of NYPD. I shared that with the mayor. The mayor once again said we will not be detaining him.” Mullin also said he spoke with New York Gov. Kathy Hochul. Belgal was the subject of a DHS investigation into the shooting of a Customs and Border Protection agent and was part of a gang “known for theft using weapons,” according to Marcos Charles, ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations executive associate director, who added that he had previously evaded federal immigration agents in September. Mamdani offered to have the NYPD take the lead on an investigation into the incident, he told Trump and Mullin. The NYPD would take over as long as federal agents left the area of the incident that evening. Trump pressed Mamdani to let the NYPD arrest Belgal, but Mamdani would not budge. A source familiar with the conversations told CNN there was no legal reason to hold Belgal without a warrant. “There was no warrant out for his arrest, no legal basis for the NYPD to take him into custody,” the person said. Negotiations broke down after that. “The mayor was being cordial, but unrealistic,” Mullin said Friday on Fox News. Aides to the mayor argue his relationship with the president has yielded significant results. Although ICE has ramped up enforcement, the agency has not carried out large-scale operations like those in Michigan or Minnesota. Mamdani arrived near the scene of the incident for a late-night press conference, during which he accused ICE of being “rotten to its core.” “Today’s shooting is only further devastating confirmation of what we have long known: that ICE operates with impunity, that they sow chaos and terror across our country, that they have killed far more of our neighbors than they could ever have claimed to save,” Mamdani said. In a press conference Friday morning, Mullin tied Mamdani and New York City’s sanctuary policies, which set limits on cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, to the incident. ICE operations in New York have been ongoing for months. An immigration enforcement operation that took place from late July to late August yielded more than 2,100 arrests, according to DHS. Mullin traveled to New York to announce the results of the operation, known as Operation Rotten Apple, and applauded ICE agents, while again criticizing Mamdani and Hochul. “Over the course of this operation, we arrested murderers, rapists, pedophiles, drug traffickers and violent assailants. And we did it with no help from Mayor Mamdani and Governor Hochul. The Trump administration is committed to protecting the American people in every city and every state, and we won’t let sanctuary politicians stand in our way,” he said . Federal data reveals that arrests in the state increased over the summer. In May, ICE took 922 people into custody in New York. That jumped to 1,190 people in June and to 1,552 in July, according to the Deportation Data Project . CNN’s Kaitlan Collins and Alayna Treene contributed to this report.

title: Trump asks Supreme Court to revive his 2016 election lawsuit against Hillary Clinton
content: President Donald Trump urged the Supreme Court on Friday to wade into his years long legal battle with former Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton and ex-Justice Department officials over the 2016 election, appealing a case that a lower court concluded was “frivolous.” Trump filed the lawsuit in 2022 against Clinton, the Democratic National Committee and dozens of other people and entities he said conspired to undermine his 2016 campaign by falsely tying him to Russia. A federal district court dismissed the suit and ultimately ruled that Trump’s attorneys were liable for nearly $1 million in sanctions. The Atlanta-based 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals largely upheld that decision last year. “This case should never have been brought. Its inadequacy as a legal claim was evident from the start,” wrote US District Judge Donald Middlebrooks of the Southern District of Florida, who was nominated to the bench by former President Bill Clinton. “No reasonable lawyer would have filed it.” Trump’s case was dismissed in part because, the district court said, his civil racketeering claims were filed too late. In his appeal to the Supreme Court, the president argues that he made a decision to wait until he was out of office. The appeal raises a question of whether a president’s responsibilities warrant holding off on certain legal deadlines while he is in office. “Faced with this conspiracy during his term, President Trump concluded that any private civil lawsuit would consume substantial time and energy and that any civil suit should therefore be postponed until after his term,” the president’s attorneys told the Supreme Court, according to a copy of the appeal reviewed by CNN. The district court “erroneously rejected the president’s theory,” Trump’s attorneys argued, “improperly treated its advocacy as evidence of nonexistent ‘bad faith,’ and relied on it to mistakenly impose sanctions.” The Supreme Court will likely decide later this year whether to hear the case.

title: Trump selects Katie Zacharia as next White House press secretary
content: President Donald Trump has selected Katie Zacharia, a conservative commentator who worked briefly at the Department of Homeland Security, as his new press secretary. Zacharia thanked Trump in a social media post Friday, writing, “Serving President Trump and the American people at this critical 250-year mark is the honor of a lifetime.” In announcing her selection earlier Friday, Trump highlighted her work for Truth Social, the Trump Media & Technology Group and her frequent appearances on Fox and Newsmax. “She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning,” he added. Trump in recent days called a number of his close allies and advisers, including former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to seek their opinion of Zacharia, a person familiar with the discussions said. And the president sought Leavitt’s counsel before making a final decision and offering Zacharia the position, they said. Zacharia told Fox News on Friday evening she will start the job on Monday, but she did not say when the first White House press briefing would be. In recounting how she got the position, Zacharia said the president “loved what a fighter I was for him.” “I got a wonderful phone call from the chief talent recruiter, the president himself, and it turns out that being a huge supporter of all of his policies actually works,” she said. Her appearance on Fox News came as Trump delivered remarks in Syracuse, New York. Zacharia was in the Oval Office with Trump earlier Friday morning, according to a person familiar. Zacharia’s selection came about quickly. As of last week, she was not being considered for the role, another person familiar said. Throughout the search to replace Leavitt, the White House struggled with higher-profile names, several of whom had previously criticized Trump. On multiple occasions, senior officials had narrowed down the list, only to find that candidates had said something negative about the president, disqualifying them from the position, according a White House official. “The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our Country and communicating to the American people the major wins that this Administration is making every single day,” Zacharia wrote on X. “I look forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out,” she said, adding that “following the fabulous Karoline Leavitt is a high standard, and one worth meeting.” Leavitt congratulated Zacharia on social media , writing, “As I told the President, Katie has my full support and I will be cheering for her and the entire team at the White House every day.” Zacharia’s been a frequent guest on Fox, Newsmax and CNN. “She’s a friend of most of you,” Trump told reporters while leaving the White House on Friday. “I know she likes people — she likes all of you. Actually, I don’t know if that’s good or bad, but we just hired a new press secretary, and she’s going to be, I think, terrific.” Zacharia served as a senior communications adviser at the Trump Media and Technology Group and Truth Social since June, which followed a two-month stint as a senior official at the Department of Homeland Security — experiences that Trump also highlighted in his social media post, along with her work in his campaigns. Zacharia, who has young children and lives in California, commuted back and forth to Washington when she was filling in at DHS. At the time, she told a friend the commute was not sustainable, according to a source familiar with the matter. Zacharia has also served as a legal adviser for Fix California, a conservative group founded by Trump ally Richard Grenell. She first came to Washington as an intern for the Republican National Committee during the George W. Bush administration in 2006. This story has been updated with additional reporting.

title: Parties prepare for byelection in Farage seat amid speculation over £5m gift inquiry
content: Nigel Farage’s rivals are gearing up for a byelection in Clacton in the months ahead, amid speculation that the standards inquiry into his £5m gift is nearing a conclusion. Conservative sources said the party was ready to fight in Farage’s seat, although senior figures in the shadow cabinet are divided about whether it would be winnable, given Farage’s victory in a byelection over the summer . Other parties, including the hard-right Restore Britain, are also expected to put up candidates in the seat this time, after boycotting the August poll. Westminster is poised for a battle over the future of Reform if the sanction from the standards inquiry is a heavy one. The process could theoretically take place before Christmas if a decision is imminent, but the timelines of previous cases suggest it is more likely to be next year – if a serious sanction is imposed. In the cases of Margaret Ferrier, the SNP MP who broke lockdown rules, and Peter Bone, the Tory MP found to have bullied staff, it took well over six months from the conclusion of the commissioner’s report for a byelection to take place. The investigation into Farage’s gift began after the Guardian revealed in May that the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024. The Reform leader has said it was a personal matter , not political, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament. Under the process, if a serious breach is found, the commissioner will pass a memorandum to the standards committee of MPs and lay members. They would then have further discussions and call a further hearing or invite evidence from the MP before deciding on a penalty. That process can take weeks. The MP also has a right of appeal to the independent expert panel, which can take a further month or more. If parliament agrees with a penalty of more than 10 days of suspension from the House of Commons , a recall petition could be held, requiring signatures from 10% of voters in the MP’s constituency over a period of six weeks. In the cases of Bone and Ferrier, neither contested their seats, and Conservatives are hopeful that Farage could decide not to fight. “There’s a question of whether he will stand again,” said one shadow cabinet minister. But Reform sources insisted Farage would fight for his seat again, having won the byelection against independent candidates including Count Binface by more than 11,000 votes. He has also recently embarked on a tour of the country, in an attempt to shore up his core support, and a reorganisation of his party HQ. This includes launching a new Reform TV channel to pump out the party’s message direct to voters, hiring a team of 12 “journalists” headed by the former GB News producer Aaron Lobo, who had been director of operations. Farage won a majority of 8,000 at the last general election, when he beat the sitting Tory MP, Giles Watling. The Conservative had previously won the seat with a majority of more than 25,000 in 2019, when there was no Brexit party candidate in the seat.

title: Tories overstate net zero cost by nearly £500bn in apparent spreadsheet error
content: Kemi Badenoch’s flagship party conference policy document overestimated the cost of net zero by nearly £500bn, seemingly after someone accidentally double-counted figures on a spreadsheet. The apparent error appears in a chapter on net zero in The Right Way , a 100-page policy document produced for the Conservative conference in Birmingham. Badenoch repeatedly used the phrase in her main speech . Justifying the Conservatives’ decision to scrap the target of the UK reaching net zero emissions by 2050, introduced under Theresa May, the document says that estimates of how much this would cost the economy “have varied enormously”. It goes on: “In 2020, the Climate Change Committee (CCC) estimated that its route to net zero would cost £957bn.” It cites the Sixth Carbon Budget produced by the CCC, the government’s climate change advisers, saying the report put gross economic costs at £1.4tn, falling to £957bn when savings were taken into account. However, the figures in the report in fact total £478bn, half of what the Tory document said. The error appears to have arisen because a tally of all the costs in a CCC spreadsheet from the document also included the row showing totals for each individual column, thus doubling it. A CCC spokesperson said: “We don’t recognise this number. The committee has previously offered to meet with Ms Badenoch and talk her through our advice. That offer is, of course, still open.” The committee’s most recent analysis puts the expected cost of achieving net zero by 2050 at about £110bn, or about £4bn a year – 0.2% of GDP. The error was spotted by the publication Carbon Brief, which informed the Guardian. It is possible the Conservatives copied the figure without checking it. It appears to have been published in a report by the rightwing thinktank the Institute of Economic Affairs and also included in an article in the Spectator. The Conservative document says it is intended to be a precise diagnosis of the UK’s problems. It is modelled in part on The Right Approach, produced by Margaret Thatcher’s Tory party in 1976, which set out some of the economic ideas later used in the 1979 election. In a foreword, Badenoch notes that “as an engineer”, she is used to correctly diagnosing issues so they can be addressed. A later part of the report says: “To fix a problem we must first have an accurate understanding of what is causing it.” The Conservatives and Badenoch’s office were contacted for comment.
